This module includes content that may be sensitive. You can check it out by yourself first. This will prepare you well for sharing the content with your teen and others afterwards.

rows.text_1_facilitator:
Teens spend lots of time online to learn, have fun, and connect with friends. It can help them grow, but also brings risks.
As caregivers, we may not know every new app — what matters most is showing interest and building a trusting relationship with our teens.

text_1_facilitator.eng:
Teens spend lots of time online to learn, have fun, and connect with friends. It can help them grow, but also brings risks.
As caregivers, we may not know every new app — what matters most is showing interest and building a trusting relationship with our teens.

text_2.eng: When we listen and guide with care, through small daily moments instead of big once-off conversations, our teens feel safe to share.

media_title.eng: Why is discussing online safety with your teen important? Click play to find out

media_transcript.eng:
Our teens spend a lot of time online — watching videos, learning, and chatting with friends. The internet can be a great place to learn and connect, but it also comes with risks.

Did you know 1 in 3 young people have been bullied online? Some are even pressured to share private photos or personal information.

We can’t stop everything that happens online. But we can listen, stay calm, and let our teens know they can always come to us. When they feel safe to talk to us, we can help them stay safer.

rows.text_2: When we listen and guide with care, through small daily moments instead of big once-off conversations, our teens feel safe to share.

rows.media_transcript:
Our teens spend a lot of time online — watching videos, learning, and chatting with friends. The internet can be a great place to learn and connect, but it also comes with risks.

Did you know 1 in 3 young people have been bullied online? Some are even pressured to share private photos or personal information.

We can’t stop everything that happens online. But we can listen, stay calm, and let our teens know they can always come to us. When they feel safe to talk to us, we can help them stay safer.

rows.text_1_facilitator:
When we explore the online world together, we understand our teens better. It shows them that online safety is about trust and support, not control.
Learning simple steps as a family builds confidence and helps teens make good choices.

text_1_facilitator.eng:
When we explore the online world together, we understand our teens better. It shows them that online safety is about trust and support, not control.
Learning simple steps as a family builds confidence and helps teens make good choices.

media_title.eng: Hear how @data.characters.media_male_1.name learned to talk to his son about online safety

media_transcript.eng:
My son was always on his phone, but I did not pay too much attention to it. To be honest, I was busy with other things and happy he was safely at home and not out on the streets. The only time we spoke about his phone was when I was taking it away as punishment for something he did. 

The SinovuyoApp helped me realize that the online world is big and can have good and bad sides. We can now talk about what he does online, and we have created rules together to ensure he can enjoy his time online and still stay safe. His phone is no longer a punishment tool but a way we can connect.

rows.media_transcript:

The SinovuyoApp helped me realize that the online world is big and can have good and bad sides. text_1_facilitator.eng: For teens, the online world feels just as real and important as the offline world.

quiz_1_question.eng: Would you let your teen experience a big new city by themselves? Would you let your teen experience the big online world by themselves?

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: It’s great that you trust your teen. There are also many risks, so we need to make sure we guide both our boys and girls to stay safe.

quiz_1_feedback_2.eng: Protecting our children shows care. Teen girls and boys also need space to learn and grow. By guiding them, we can balance safety and independence.

quiz_1_feedback_3.eng: Parenting online is not easy. By carefully giving freedom while offering guidance, you can help your son or daughter learn while staying safe.

rows.text_1_facilitator:
Sometimes teens run into tricky or even dangerous situations online, and as caregivers it’s not always easy to know what to do.

Let’s look at 5 examples of online warning signs and how we can support our teens.

text_1_facilitator.eng:
Sometimes teens run into tricky or even dangerous situations online, and as caregivers it’s not always easy to know what to do.

Let’s look at 5 examples of online warning signs and how we can support our teens.

text_2.eng: **Warning Sign 1: Lerato is quiet and withdrawn — a change in mood can signal something is wrong.**

character_1_text.eng: (_thinking_) I am so worried about Lerato. She has been acting differently lately. She seems quiet and keeps to herself.

quiz_1_question.eng: What could be signs that something is wrong?

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: Yes, these can be signs that something is wrong. What looks like teen behaviour can sometimes mean your teen feels unsafe. When strangers give attention online, teens may feel excited or special at first. Spending time together and showing interest in who your teen talks to helps you notice changes early.

rows.text_2: **Warning Sign 2: @data.characters.f3_daughter_12.name hears about a classmate sharing private photos — hearing such stories is a warning sign to talk with your teen about pressure and safety online.**

text_2.eng: **Warning Sign 2: @data.characters.f3_daughter_12.name hears about a classmate sharing private photos — hearing such stories is a warning sign to talk with your teen about pressure and safety online.**

character_1_text.eng: Mother, guess what happened at school. My classmate @data.characters.friend_female_5.name shared a sexy picture of herself with her boyfriend to prove that she loves him, and his friends told him to post it online. Now it is everywhere.

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng:
Yes, these are all good responses. By thanking teens and responding supportively, they are more likely to share their own problems. 
Remind them to only share photos with permission, think about consequences, and that bullying and sharing private content is harmful. Support them to take safe steps, like reporting and deleting.

rows.text_2: **Warning Sign 3: @data.characters.f1_son_18.name is being threatened online — fear and threats are warning signs of sexual exploitation or blackmail.** _This happens when someone says they will share private photos or messages to scare or control someone._

text_2.eng: **Warning Sign 3: @data.characters.f1_son_18.name is being threatened online — fear and threats are warning signs of sexual exploitation or blackmail.** _This happens when someone says they will share private photos or messages to scare or control someone._

character_1_text.eng: Send me another picture or I’ll share the last one with your family and friends…

character_2_text.eng: (_thinking_): What if my friends and family see those other pictures I sent… I don’t know what to do! Maybe I should talk to my father.

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: This may feel like protecting @data.characters.f1_son_18.name, but it can push him to hide problems and stop him from telling you next time. Taking the phone does not solve the danger.

quiz_1_feedback_2.eng: Blaming breaks trust. Teens make mistakes, and feeling ashamed can make the situation worse. What matters most is helping @data.characters.f1_son_18.name feel safe and supported.

quiz_1_feedback_3.eng: Yes! Stay calm and listen. Tell @data.characters.f1_son_18.name it’s not his fault. Block and report if you can, and plan together what to do if photos are shared. If there’s anyone you both trust, ask them for help.

quiz_2_question.eng: Can this happen to boys and girls?

quiz_2_feedback_1.eng:
Both boys and girls can face this kind of online threat, but boys may ask for help less often because they feel ashamed.
This is a serious and unsafe situation. Remind your teen that it is not their fault and no one deserves to be threatened. Tell them to stop sending pictures, save the messages as proof, and speak to a trusted adult right away.

rows.text_2: **Warning Sign 4: @data.characters.f2_son_15.name shared private pictures at school — sharing or showing private or harmful images is a warning sign that teens need clear guidance.**

text_2.eng: **Warning Sign 4: @data.characters.f2_son_15.name shared private pictures at school — sharing or showing private or harmful images is a warning sign that teens need clear guidance.**

character_1_text.eng: Why is your grandson showing my daughter those pictures at school!

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: Denying the problem may feel easier, but it makes the situation worse. It is better to face the issue calmly, so you can understand what happened and give both children the support they need.

quiz_1_feedback_2.eng: Saying “boys will be boys” makes harmful behaviour seem normal. This stops children from understanding the real consequences of their actions.

quiz_1_feedback_3.eng: Getting very angry can shame your teen and close the door to learning. He may only feel fear, without understanding why it was wrong.

quiz_1_feedback_4.eng: Correct. By staying calm and listening, you help your teen feel safe to talk. This gives you a chance to explain why sharing sexual pictures or videos is harmful and guide him to make better choices in the future.

quiz_2_question.eng: Are sexual pictures or videos only shared by boys?

quiz_2_feedback_1.eng:
Both boys and girls can be involved in this.
Teach your teen to respect others and ask before sharing photos or videos. Explain that sharing or watching sexual content can hurt people.
Remind them it’s illegal to share any nude or sexual images of anyone under 18 — even their own.

rows.text_2: **Warning Sign 5: @data.characters.f2_son_15.name gets a message from a stranger while showing his grandpa his game. When strangers offer gifts or ask to chat, it’s a warning sign.**

text_2.eng: **Warning Sign 5: @data.characters.f2_son_15.name gets a message from a stranger while showing his grandpa his game. When strangers offer gifts or ask to chat, it’s a warning sign.**

character_1_text.eng: I saw your profile. We are at the same school! Let’s chat privately — maybe we can plan how to meet in person. I’ll send you data.

quiz_1_question.eng: What would you do if you were @data.characters.f2_son_15.name’s grandfather?

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: Ignoring the problem may seem easiest, but it can put teens in danger. Strangers can use personal details from a profile as well as gifts to trick or pressure children.

quiz_1_feedback_2.eng: Yes! Ask @data.characters.f2_son_15.name what happened, what information he shared, and how he felt. Then guide him on safe choices like keeping profiles private and not replying to strangers.

quiz_1_feedback_3.eng: Getting angry may scare @data.characters.f2_son_15.name and shut down openness. He may hide future problems instead of asking for help. Stay calm so he knows he can trust you.

quiz_1_feedback_4.eng: Forcing may feel like protecting @data.characters.f2_son_15.name, but it can break trust and lead him to hide things in the future. A better way is to sit together, talk through the risks, and agree on safe solutions as a team.

quiz_1_feedback_5.eng: That’s right! Use this as a chance to explain why accepting gifts or sharing personal details (like school or uniform) online is unsafe. Explore together how to block and report strangers, and remind your teen they can always come to you if something feels wrong.

rows.text_1_facilitator: Keeping your teen safe online starts with understanding their experiences. Let’s come up with easy ways to get involved in your teen’s world online.

text_1_facilitator.eng: Keeping your teen safe online starts with understanding their experiences. Let’s come up with easy ways to get involved in your teen’s world online.

text_2.eng:
**Here are some examples of shared online moments:**

🖥️ Watch a short video or song together
💜 Share memes and funny clips
😊 Ask your teen to teach you something online (like posting a family photo)
💬 Ask “Did you see anything fun or interesting online today?” 
📓 Help with research or homework online

rows.text_1_facilitator: Here are some tips to help you with online safety:

text_1_facilitator.eng: Here are some tips to help you with online safety:

section_1_text.eng:
Show interest in what your teen does online and listen without judging.

Talk about safe boundaries, such as only chatting online with people they know in real life. If something goes wrong, stay calm and remind them they can always come to you. Teens share more when they feel safe and trusted.

section_1_extra_text.eng: Ask your teen what they would do if a friend was in danger online. Remind them it’s okay to involve a trusted adult.

section_2_text.eng:
Remind your teen to think before posting. 💭
Once something is online, it can spread fast and be hard to delete. 

Remind them to always be kind and respectful online, and to ask before sharing anyone’s photo or information — and show this by doing it yourself. Private or sexual pictures should never be shared.

section_2_extra_text.eng: Encourage your teen to remind friends to stay safe too — friends can help friends make good choices.

section_3_text.eng:
Watch for warning signs, like mood changes, hiding phone, sudden extra time online. This can happen when someone online asks for photos, secrets, or offers gifts like money or airtime.

If something unsafe happens, don’t blame or punish your teen. Stay calm and help them block the person, report the problem, and delete sensitive photos or messages they shared.

If your teen has hurt others online, stay calm. Help them learn and do better — without shame or anger.

section_3_extra_text.eng:
**Deleting** means removing content (like a photo or message).
**Reporting** means telling the app about the problem (for example on Facebook or TikTok).

Remind your teen they can always ask for help if something feels wrong. They can ask you, a teacher, another trusted adult, or contact Childline (call 116).

section_4_text.eng: Set accounts to private, turn off location sharing, and use strong passwords. Remind your teen not to share their full name, phone number, home address, school name, or photos in school uniform. Explore together how to block and report anyone who makes them feel uncomfortable.

section_4_extra_text.eng: Parental controls and online safety are confusing! Talk with other caregivers, research ways to keep your child safe, and talk about it together.

rows.text_1_facilitator:
This week’s activity is to make an Online Family Agreement with your teen. 

When you create rules together, teens feel part of the team — not controlled — and are more likely to follow them.

text_1_facilitator.eng:
This week’s activity is to make an Online Family Agreement with your teen. 

When you create rules together, teens feel part of the team — not controlled — and are more likely to follow them.

text_2.eng:
**Sit with your teen and make 5 rules for safe and fun online time.
Stick them on the wall when you’re done!**
👩‍👩‍👦 When both caregivers join in, your teen sees that everyone helps keep the family safe ❤️.

**Sample Online Family Agreement**

Our family agrees to these rules for safe and fun online time:
🔑 Keep accounts private
🚩 Do not share school, address, or phone number
✅ Ask permission before sharing photos of others
⏰ No phones during meals or at bedtime
☀️ Be kind and respectful to others online
😃 Share one positive or funny post or video with the family each week
💛 Teens: I will talk to an adult if anything feels wrong or uncomfortable online
✨ Caregivers: I will listen and support my teens without judging or blaming

Signed by:
🔶 Parent / Caregiver __________
🔷 Teen __________

quiz_1_question.eng: Can you create and try out your Online Family Agreement this week?

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: Making the agreement together shows your teen that online safety is about teamwork. You can always change or update your agreement later as well.

quiz_1_feedback_2.eng: Give it a try. Involving your teen in choosing the rules helps them feel respected and makes it more likely they will follow them. You can start with just one rule and add more later.

quiz_1_feedback_3.eng: That’s okay. You can start small. Even agreeing on just one rule together is a good first step. You can always add more ideas later on.

rows.text_1_facilitator:
Online risks can look different for boys and girls. They may hide or act out in different ways. When we blame or punish, they stop sharing — and the risk grows.

You don’t need to know everything. The best way to keep your teen safe is to build trust, stay calm, and let them know they can always come to you for help.

media_title.eng: Hear how @data.characters.media_daughter_9.name’s mother helped her keep safe online

media_transcript.eng: Someone took my photo and put it on a naked body in a video. I freaked out and didn’t want to tell anyone, because I thought my parents would just take my phone away. But when my mom saw I was upset and asked, she stayed calm. We reported it together and made a plan on what to do next. I told my friends it was a fake, and my family did the same. I felt like everyone was on my side. Now I know I don't have to deal with things like this by myself.
